title: From Southern Cross to Pole Star: the Swiss Schoolmaster, Mancha and Gato, and the Length of the Americas
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Bern, birth into an old Swiss family
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the seventh of May a son is born in Bern to an old Swiss family and named Aimé Félix Tschiffely. The city stands on a loop of the Aare under arcades of stone, ringed by mountains that close the horizon. He is schooled in Switzerland and trained as a teacher, the trade his family expects of him. No consulted source records anything of his first twenty years that would account for what he does with the next thirty. He is born landlocked, in a country that has no plain.
suggested_refs: Bern civil registers for 7 May 1895; the Tschiffely family of Bern

stops.name: England, the ring and the schoolroom
stops.date_confidence: inferred; no consulted source dates the English years, names a club, or names a school. The pin is London as a placeholder for England, not an attested address
stops.campa: Before he settles into schoolmastering he tries a spell as a professional footballer and a spell as a boxer, then crosses to England and teaches. No source reachable here names the clubs, the opponents or the schools, and none gives a year for any of it. A trained teacher keeps putting his body against other tests before he consents to the desk, and the same man will one day ask two old geldings to do what every horseman he knows says horses cannot do. England holds him briefly. Argentina is advertising for masters who can teach in English.
suggested_refs: English school registers of the 1910s for a Swiss-born master named Tschiffely: not located

stops.name: St. George's College, Quilmes: the Anglo-Argentine post
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the appointment is attested, the year is not given in any consulted source
stops.campa: He takes a teaching post at St. George's College in Quilmes, an English foundation on the flat land south of Buenos Aires, where the sons of the Anglo-Argentine merchant families are taught cricket, Latin and the habits of an England most of them have never seen. Outside the playing fields the province runs off to the horizon in every direction, and the horizon is worked by men on horseback. The Swiss master, who learned to ride nowhere in particular, begins spending his holidays in the saddle on the pampa.
suggested_refs: St. George's College, Guido 800, Quilmes: staff records of the early 1920s

stops.name: Belgrano, temporary headmaster of the Buenos Aires English High School
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the headmastership is attested without a date. The school has stood at Melián 1880, Belgrano, since 1906, which fixes the site for his tenure
stops.campa: He serves as temporary headmaster of the Buenos Aires English High School in Belgrano, and uses the school vacations to ride and explore the pampas. This is the same Anglo and European facing Buenos Aires that Victoria Ocampo's circle curates for its lecturers, the city that will receive Keyserling four years later under her patronage. Tschiffely belongs to its schoolroom rather than its salon. He is a foreign master with long holidays and a growing collection of maps, and he has not yet said the idea aloud to anybody who would repeat it.
suggested_refs: Buenos Aires English High School, Melián 1880, Belgrano: headmasters' list
sources: The Long Riders' Guild author page

stops.name: Chubut, Solanet buys the herd from a cacique
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1911; month and day are not given, and the cacique's ground in western Chubut is reconstructed, no source supplying coordinates
stops.campa: The criollo breeder Emilio Solanet travels down into Patagonia and buys some ninety mares and stallions from a Tehuelche cacique on the Chubut steppe. The animals are small, thick-necked, roman-nosed and unbeautiful by every English standard of the show ring, and they have survived generations on frozen grass with no shelter and no grain. Among them is the stock from which two geldings will come, a skewbald and a dun. Solanet is buying a bloodline that Argentina is close to breeding out of existence in favour of imported blood.
suggested_refs: Emilio Solanet's Patagonian purchase of 1911 and the Tehuelche criollo stock
sources: La Nación, 'La épica de Mancha y Gato: los caballos criollos que cruzaron América hace 100 años' (2025)

stops.name: Estancia El Cardal, Ayacucho: the two geldings are handed over
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1925; no source gives the month of the handover
stops.campa: At his estancia near Ayacucho in Buenos Aires province, Solanet gives Tschiffely two aged criollo geldings: Mancha, an overo rosado of about fifteen, and Gato, a gateado of about sixteen, both raised on the Chubut steppe. Solanet is among the founders of the Asociación de Criadores de Caballos Criollos, established at a general assembly of breeders on 16 June 1923 under its first president Raúl Videla Dorna, and he wants the breed proved in public. He hands the two geldings over as a gift, with one condition attached: that the argument be made where it can be seen.
stops.quote: Their sturdy legs, short thick necks and Roman noses are as far removed from the points of a first-class English hunter as the North Pole from the South. Handsome is as handsome does, however, and I am willing to state my opinion boldly that no other breed in the world has the capacity of the Criollo for continuous hard work.
stops.quote_source: A.F. Tschiffely, Tschiffely's Ride (1933), quoted in Horse Canada, 'Tschiffely and the 10,000-Mile, Three-Year Ride: Part I of II'
suggested_refs: Estancia El Cardal, Ayacucho, and the founding acts of the Asociación de Criadores de Caballos Criollos, 16 June 1923
sources: La Nación, 'La épica de Mancha y Gato...' (2025)

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the city hears the plan
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the press reaction is undated tradition, and this is the atlas's canonical Buenos Aires pin rather than a located address
stops.campa: The plan reaches the papers before the horses reach the road: a Swiss schoolmaster intends to ride to Washington. This is the pin the atlas already shares with Borges, Victoria Ocampo, Eva Perón, Juan Perón, Che Guevara, Emin Arslan, Charly García and Spinetta, and almost every one of them stands on it as an arrival or a residence. Tschiffely stands on it as a gate. Four years later Keyserling will land here on Ocampo's invitation to lecture on the world; Tschiffely proposes instead to go and see the length of it at four miles an hour.
stops.quote: a lunatic proposing to ride overland to New York
stops.quote_source: Attributed to an unnamed 1925 Buenos Aires newspaper, repeated in Long Riders' Guild material and book blurbs; no source consulted names the paper or gives a dated citation, so the wording is tradition rather than attestation
suggested_refs: Buenos Aires press of April 1925 on the announced ride: the specific notice is not located
sources: The Long Riders' Guild promotional material for Tschiffely's Ride

stops.name: Sociedad Rural Argentina, Palermo: the ride begins
stops.date_confidence: contested: English and Spanish Wikipedia give 23 or 24 April 1925, La Nación (2025) gives 20 April. The disagreement is not resolved here
stops.campa: He rides out of the Sociedad Rural grounds in Palermo on two horses nobody expects to see again, bound for Washington, D.C., something like ten thousand miles north. He carries a saddle, a revolver, a camera and no support party. A veterinarian has told him the animals will break down inside a few hundred kilometres. Solanet's whole argument rides with them; so does the professional reputation of a man who until this month was a headmaster. He is thirty years old, and by his own account not calm.
stops.quote: assailed by a sickly feeling, as if my stomach were a vacuum
stops.quote_source: A.F. Tschiffely, Tschiffely's Ride (1933), quoted in Horse Canada, 'Tschiffely and the 10,000-Mile, Three-Year Ride: Part I of II'
suggested_refs: The predio ferial of the Sociedad Rural Argentina, Av. Sarmiento 2704, Palermo
sources: Mónica Stork, 'La travesía de Gato y Mancha', Información Veterinaria (Córdoba) 166:60 (2011)

stops.name: Rosario, past the veterinarian's prediction
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the stop is attested, the date is not
stops.campa: The party reaches Rosario on the Paraná already past the distance at which the horses were promised to fail. Nothing has failed. Tschiffely is learning the two animals the way a man learns two colleagues, and finding them opposite in almost everything: one suspicious, territorial and hard-mouthed, the other quick to give in and take the world as it comes. The road north from here leaves the fat country and starts drying out. He is writing the differences down as he goes, in a notebook that will become a book.
stops.quote: Desde los primeros días advertí una real diferencia entre sus personalidades. Mancha era un excelente perro guardián: estaba siempre alerta, desconfiaba de los extraños y no permitía que hombre alguno, aparte de mí mismo, lo montase... Gato era un caballo de carácter muy distinto. Fue domado con mayor rapidez que su compañero. Cuando descubrió que los corcovos y todo su repertorio de aviesos recursos para arrojarme al suelo fracasaban, se resignó a su destino y tomó las cosas filosóficamente... Mancha dominaba completamente a Gato, que nunca tomaba represalias
stops.quote_source: A.F. Tschiffely, Spanish edition (translator not named on the source page), quoted verbatim in Mónica Stork, 'La travesía de Gato y Mancha', Información Veterinaria (Córdoba) 166:60 (2011)
suggested_refs: Infobae, 'La osada travesía de Gato y Mancha' (20 September 2025)
sources: Infobae, 'La osada travesía de Gato y Mancha' (2025)

stops.name: Santiago del Estero, the locust swarm
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the episode is attested to the 1925 northward leg without a date
stops.campa: Crossing Santiago del Estero the three of them ride into a locust swarm, the sky going brown and solid and the insects hitting horse and rider like thrown gravel. The province is thorn scrub and salt flat, hot beyond the pampa's heat, and the water is far apart. Tschiffely does not turn aside for the swarm and does not lose an animal to it, and the route north is not altered by a metre. The Andean foothills are already visible to the west as a change in the light.
suggested_refs: Literary Traveler, 'Tschiffely's Epic Ride'

stops.name: San Miguel de Tucumán, the last city before the climb
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the stop appears in route summaries without a date
stops.campa: Tucumán is the last large Argentine city on the road, sugar country under green hills, and after it the route goes up. The horses have crossed the whole width of the republic's northern plain on grass and whatever the road offered. Tschiffely never ties them at night. He sleeps in whatever hut is offered and turns them loose outside it, and in the morning they are at the door. The habit will hold for the whole three years of the road, and he will need neither picket line nor paddock on any of it.
stops.quote: Mis dos caballos me querían tanto que nunca debí atarlos, y hasta cuando dormía en alguna choza solitaria, sencillamente los dejaba sueltos, seguro de que nunca se alejarían más de algunos metros y de que me aguardarían en la puerta a la mañana siguiente, cuando me saludaban con un cordial relincho.
stops.quote_source: A.F. Tschiffely, Spanish edition, quoted in Mónica Stork, 'La travesía de Gato y Mancha' (2011); the Stork PDF prints 'nuca se alejarían', corrected here from veterinariargentina.com, which reads 'nunca'
suggested_refs: Route summaries of the 1925 Argentine leg via Tucumán
sources: WebSearch summary of Wikipedia and Infobae route accounts

stops.name: Tres Cruces, the pass at eleven thousand feet
stops.date_confidence: contested and partly reconstructed: the source names a Tres Cruces pass and gives eleven thousand feet, calling it Bolivian, but the only pass matching altitude and itinerary is Tres Cruces on RN9 in Jujuy, Argentina, at about 3,693 m. The Bolivian Abra Tres Cruces lies far north in La Paz department at 4,729 m. The country label in the source is probably wrong; the coordinates here are the Jujuy pass
stops.campa: At eleven thousand feet the riders take nosebleeds and hail comes down the size of eggs. Above the tree line the criollos are working in air that no lowland horse tolerates, and they are eating what the puna offers, which is coarse tufted grass and very little of it. Tschiffely walks as much as he rides. Behind him, seven hundred kilometres south along this same wall of rock, San Martín took an army over the cordillera in 1817; the same mountains that made a nation are now simply the second obstacle on a road with most of its countries still ahead of it.
suggested_refs: Tres Cruces, Jujuy, on RN9, and the Abra Tres Cruces of the Quimsa Cruz range, Bolivia: the two candidates for the source's pass
sources: Horse Canada, 'Tschiffely and the 10,000-Mile, Three-Year Ride: Part I'

stops.name: Potosí, the silver city on the road north
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the stop is attested, the date is not
stops.campa: Potosí stands under the Cerro Rico, the mountain whose silver paid for two centuries of Spanish Europe and killed the men who dug it. Tschiffely rides in on two horses from a Tehuelche herd, through a city built by the empire that the Tehuelche outlived. He is on the altiplano proper now, above thirteen thousand feet, where the cold is dry and the nights are lethal. The worst climb of the entire route lies immediately north, on the road toward Challapata, and nobody has told him what it will measure.
suggested_refs: Stork 2011 on the Potosí to Challapata leg

stops.name: Paso El Cóndor, the altitude record
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the crossing is reported without a date, and no consulted source gives coordinates for the pass. The pin is interpolated between Potosí and Challapata
stops.campa: Between Potosí and Challapata the road tops out at a height reported as 5,900 metres, and Mancha and Gato are said to set a world altitude record for mounted travel that has not been claimed since. The figure comes from a single line of veterinary reporting and no survey supports it. The ground is the same whatever the figure: no fodder, no shelter, no oxygen worth the name, and two horses in their sixteenth and seventeenth years walking over it. On the far side the altiplano road runs down to Challapata and the lake country.
stops.quote: For a moment I watched in horror and then the miracle happened. A solitary sturdy tree stopped his slide towards certain death...
stops.quote_source: A.F. Tschiffely, Tschiffely's Ride (1933), quoted in Horse Canada, 'Tschiffely and the 10,000-Mile, Three-Year Ride: Part II'; the ellipsis is the quoting article's, unverified against the original page
suggested_refs: Paso El Cóndor between Potosí and Challapata: no surveyed coordinates located

stops.name: La Paz, the mayor comes out to look
stops.date_confidence: attested to the 1925 leg, roughly three weeks from the Argentine border; no calendar date is given in any consulted source
stops.campa: About three weeks out from the Argentine frontier the party comes down into the bowl of La Paz, and the mayor receives them in astonishment. The horses have crossed the highest inhabited country on the continent and are sound. Word begins to travel ahead of the rider now, by telegraph and by newspaper, so that the arrival at each next town is expected. From La Paz the route bends northwest into Peru and the old Inca road, where the passes are lower but the bridges are rope.
suggested_refs: Horse Canada, 'Tschiffely and the 10,000-Mile, Three-Year Ride: Part I'
sources: The Long Riders' Guild author page

segments.name: The Inca Road and the Sand

stops.name: Cusco, into the Inca heartland
stops.date_confidence: inferred; Cusco is named in route summaries without a date, and the year is given variously as 1925 or 1926
stops.campa: Cusco is the navel of the old empire, its Inca walls carrying Spanish churches on their backs, and the road out of it is the road the runners of the Inca used. Tschiffely follows a surface built for feet, not hooves, cut into gorge walls with drops that do not forgive a slipped shoe. The horses have to be led on the worst of it. On one such slope one of them goes over the edge and is caught by a single tree; the rider watches it happen from above and can do nothing at all.
stops.quote: Poor Gato was now neighing pitifully to his companion, who was above in safety. It was not his usual neigh, it had in it a note of desperation and fear.
stops.quote_source: A.F. Tschiffely, Tschiffely's Ride (1933), quoted in Horse Canada, Part II; the quoting source uses an en dash where a comma is substituted here
suggested_refs: The Qhapaq Ñan through the Cusco region
sources: The Long Riders' Guild author page

stops.name: Ayacucho, Peru: the rope bridges and the landslides
stops.date_confidence: attested to the Peruvian leg of 1926; no month or day is given, and the pin is the atlas's existing Ayacucho, Peru location
stops.campa: Landslides take the road out repeatedly through the Ayacucho country and the rivers are crossed on hanging bridges of woven fibre that swing and sag under a horse. Sucre broke the last royalist army of the Andes on the pampa above this town in December 1824 and finished the liberation of the continent there. Tschiffely rides through it a century later without an army, and toward a capital named for a general who never came south. There is another Ayacucho, in Buenos Aires province, where the horses were given to him and where they will die.
stops.quote: We had crossed some giddy and wobbly hanging bridges before, but here we came to the worst I had ever seen or ever wish to see again.
stops.quote_source: A.F. Tschiffely, Tschiffely's Ride (1933), quoted in Horse Canada, 'Tschiffely and the 10,000-Mile, Three-Year Ride: Part II'
suggested_refs: The Ayacucho battlefield of 9 December 1824 and the fibre bridges of the Peruvian sierra
sources: The Long Riders' Guild author page

stops.name: Lima, down from the sierra to the coast
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1926; no month or day is given in any consulted source
stops.campa: The route comes down out of the sierra to the viceregal capital on its grey coast, where the sun is a rumour for half the year and it never rains. Lima receives the rider as the cities have begun to: a reception, a photograph, a horse show. He rests the animals and looks at what comes next on the map, which is the Peruvian desert, seven hundred kilometres of it, running north between the Andes and the Pacific with the sand blowing across the road. It is the stretch that will nearly finish them.
suggested_refs: Peruvian press coverage of the 1926 arrival in Lima
sources: WebSearch summary citing the published route description

stops.name: Huarmey, the guide gives out
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1926; the La Nación dispatch quoted here is undated within the paper
stops.campa: At Huarmey the hired guide can go no further and neither can his animals. The two criollos roll in the dust, drink, and then fall on the grass with the appetites of lions. Ahead lies thirty leagues to Casma with no water and no forage. Buenos Aires is reading all of this in the paper as it happens, in dispatches that make the horses the protagonists and the Swiss schoolmaster their companion, and a country that had been importing thoroughbred blood for fifty years begins to reconsider the animals it was breeding out.
stops.quote: En Huarmey el guía no pudo más, ni sus bestias. Los dos criollos Mancha y Gato se revolcaron, tomaron agua y después se volcaron al pasto con apetitos de leones. De Huarmey a Casma, 30 leguas, calores colosales ¡52 grados a la sombra! sin agua, ni forraje, arena, arena, arena. Los cascos se hundían permanentemente de 6 a 15 pulgadas en la arena candente.
stops.quote_source: Diario La Nación (Buenos Aires), contemporary dispatch on the ride, quoted in Mónica Stork, 'La travesía de Gato y Mancha' (2011), p. 2; the exact issue date is not given on the source page
suggested_refs: The La Nación dispatches of 1925 to 1928 on the ride: original issue dates not established

stops.name: Casma, thirty leagues of hot sand
stops.date_confidence: inferred from the Huarmey dispatch, which gives the leg but no calendar date
stops.campa: Fifty-two degrees in the shade, and there is no shade. The hooves sink six to fifteen inches into sand hot enough to blister, and the crossing to Casma is made without water or fodder for either horse. The dispatch that reports it repeats one word three times, sand, and lets that stand for the country. Tschiffely comes out the far side with both animals alive. From Casma the coast road runs on north through Trujillo toward the Ecuadorian border, and the terrain changes from desert to cloud.
suggested_refs: The Huarmey to Casma desert leg on the old Peruvian coast road

stops.name: Quito, the road washes away
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1926; no month or day is given in any consulted source
stops.campa: Ecuador brings mountain again and, with it, landslides that carry the road off the hillside faster than it can be rebuilt. The approach to Quito is made through mud and around fresh scars. Humboldt climbed these volcanoes in 1802 and took their measurements to Washington two years later, where Jefferson received him at the President's House. Tschiffely will present himself at the same capital, off the same continent, with two horses instead of instruments and a claim about a breed instead of a theory about the earth.
suggested_refs: Horse Canada, 'Tschiffely and the 10,000-Mile, Three-Year Ride: Part II'

stops.name: Rumichaca, the stone bridge into Colombia
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1926; no date is given, and the coordinates are those of the Rumichaca natural bridge on the modern Ipiales-Tulcán frontier
stops.campa: The crossing from Ecuador into Colombia is made at Rumichaca, the stone bridge over the Carchi gorge that the Quechua name calls exactly what it is. It is a natural arch, not a built one, and it has carried the road between the two countries since before either country existed. The party crosses the equator somewhere behind them without ceremony. Ahead is the eastern cordillera and its long descent toward the Caribbean, and beyond that a piece of the map that has no road drawn on it at all.
suggested_refs: The Rumichaca natural bridge on the Ecuador-Colombia border

stops.name: Medellín, down the cordillera
stops.date_confidence: inferred; Medellín is named in route summaries without a date
stops.campa: Medellín sits in its valley among the coffee slopes of Antioquia, and the road to it is the long ladder down the eastern cordillera. The horses are eighteen months out of Palermo. Tschiffely rides them alternately, one packed and one under saddle, and switches every day so neither carries the weight twice running; the arrangement is the reason two animals of their age are still walking. From here the country falls away toward the swamps of the coast, and the rainy season is coming on.
suggested_refs: Route summaries of the Colombian leg via Medellín
sources: WebSearch summary citing the published route description

stops.name: Cartagena, the road ends at the water
stops.date_confidence: attested to the 1926-1927 turn; no month or day is given in any consulted source
stops.campa: By the time the party reaches the Caribbean coast the rains have set in and the country between Colombia and Panama is swamp with no road through it. The Darién is one hundred and sixty kilometres of jungle, river and mangrove that has defeated every attempt to build across it and defeats horses absolutely. Tschiffely stands at the end of the continent's road system with two thousand miles behind him and admits the obvious. Bolívar wrote from Kingston in 1815 that the isthmus might one day gather the American nations; it has not yet gathered a track.
suggested_refs: Horse Canada, Part II, on the Cartagena decision

stops.name: Miraflores, the Darién refused and the canal crossed
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1927; no month or day is given, and the six-week wait is reported without dates
stops.campa: The horses go around the Darién by sea and are landed on the Panamanian side, and the legend that Tschiffely rode the gap dies here on the record even as it starts to circulate. The American canal administration receives him as a celebrity, and he waits six weeks at the locks for the rains to break before riding on. The canal below him has cut the Americas in two at the exact place the Americas were already impassable. He resumes the ride on the far bank of an ocean-to-ocean ditch, in a country that is nineteen years old.
suggested_refs: Miraflores Locks and the Canal Zone administration's reception of Tschiffely, 1927

stops.name: San José, over the Cerro de la Muerte
stops.date_confidence: attested to 15 April 1927 by route accounts, which do not date the Cerro de la Muerte crossing itself
stops.campa: The road into the Costa Rican central valley goes over the Cerro de la Muerte, which is named for the people it has killed and earns it on the exposed section above three thousand metres, where the cloud comes down and the temperature drops. The horses fall repeatedly on the descent. On the fifteenth of April they walk into San José. Central America will take a year: five small republics, one of them at war, and a coastline where the shipping is often faster and always safer than the mule track behind the beach.
suggested_refs: The old Cerro de la Muerte trail south of San José
sources: Infobae and route summaries citing arrival in San José on 15 April 1927

stops.name: San Salvador, around the Nicaraguan war
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1927; no month or day is given in any consulted source
stops.campa: Nicaragua is in civil war and both sides are short of horses, which makes two conspicuously sound criollos a requisition waiting to happen. Tschiffely puts them on a boat and skips the country entirely, landing in El Salvador. It is the second time the ride has gone by sea, first for the jungle and now for armed men. Both horses come off the boat sound. The line on the map stays unbroken from Palermo, but two stretches of it were never walked, and he says so in the book.
suggested_refs: The 1927 Nicaraguan civil war and the Salvadorean detour
sources: WebSearch summary of route accounts on the Nicaraguan detour

stops.name: Guatemala City, the relief map at Minerva Park
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1927; no month or day is given in any consulted source
stops.campa: In Guatemala City he goes to look at the giant relief map of the republic laid out at Minerva Park, an entire country reduced to something a man can walk around in twenty minutes. He has just crossed most of it at the other scale, by way of Lake Atitlán and the village of Nahualá. Accounts of the ride give the number of countries crossed as eleven, as twenty, and as the dust of twenty nations, which was a newspaper's phrase and not a count. The sources do not agree and are not reconciled here.
suggested_refs: The Mapa en Relieve at Minerva Park, Guatemala City, built 1904
sources: The Long Riders' Guild author page

stops.name: Oaxaca, the mule's kick
stops.date_confidence: contested location: Infobae places Gato's injury at Oaxaca, with the horse then sent on to Mexico City by rail, while Stork 2011 and shorter summaries place the injury in Mexico City itself. The two accounts are not reconciled, and neither is dated
stops.campa: A mule kicks Gato and the leg is bad enough to end his ride. Where it happens is disputed: one account puts it at Oaxaca with the horse entrained north, another puts it in Mexico City. What is agreed is the consequence. Gato goes ahead by rail and waits, and Tschiffely rides the last three thousand miles on Mancha alone. Two and a half years and eleven countries have not touched either animal; a single kick in a Mexican yard does what the altiplano and the Peruvian desert could not.
suggested_refs: Infobae's Mexican itinerary: Tapachula, Mexico City, Jalisco, Oaxaca
sources: Infobae, 'La osada travesía de Gato y Mancha'

stops.name: Mexico City, the charro escort
stops.date_confidence: attested to 2 November 1927 by Infobae's Mexican itinerary
stops.campa: Mexico becomes his favourite stretch of the whole road. A charro association receives him, the press and the film men meet him, and he rides in a bullfight parade. When he leaves, a mounted escort of charros rides the first ten miles out of the capital with him: horsemen of one tradition seeing off a horseman of another, on an animal bred by a people the Argentine state had spent the century pushing off its own grass. Gato stays behind with his leg. Mancha goes north alone toward the border.
suggested_refs: Mexican charro associations and the 1927 reception in Mexico City
sources: Infobae, 'La osada travesía de Gato y Mancha'

stops.name: Laredo, Texas: across the Rio Grande
stops.date_confidence: attested as the point of entry into the United States; no calendar date is given in any consulted source, and the 1928 year is inferred from the route
stops.campa: Harassed by bandits in northern Mexico and given a military escort for part of it, Tschiffely crosses into the United States at Laredo. Some accounts route him through San Luis Potosí to get here; no source consulted attests that, and Infobae's Mexican itinerary runs by Tapachula, the capital, Jalisco and Oaxaca instead. In Texas the Rangers take him in as a guest. He is riding one horse now, on paved roads for the first time since Buenos Aires, and the paving will turn out to matter.
suggested_refs: The Long Riders' Guild account of the Texas Rangers' hospitality, 1928
sources: The Long Riders' Guild author page

stops.name: St. Louis, the Mississippi crossing
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the stop is attested, the date is not
stops.campa: The route runs from Texas up through Oklahoma and the Ozarks to St. Louis, and there the Mississippi is crossed. Asphalt is doing to the horses what mountain rock never did, and Gato, brought up to rejoin, cannot take this stretch; only Mancha crosses. Beyond the river the road goes on to Indianapolis, then Columbus, then over the Blue Ridge. A country that keeps a horse on hard surface all day is a new kind of terrain, and it is the last one on the list.
suggested_refs: The Long Riders' Guild United States itinerary: Laredo, Oklahoma, the Ozarks, St. Louis, Indianapolis, Columbus, the Blue Ridge, Washington

stops.name: Washington, D.C., received by President Coolidge
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1928; no exact date for the White House reception is given in any consulted source
stops.campa: Calvin Coolidge receives him at the White House and the National Geographic Society honours him separately. This is the capital where Miranda came to study Washington himself in 1783, where Jefferson received Humboldt in 1804, where Alvear presented credentials to Monroe in 1824 and stayed fourteen years as Argentine minister, and where Sarmiento served before being elected president from abroad. Every one of them arrived by ship. Tschiffely is the first to arrive on a horse, and the horse came from a Tehuelche herd in Chubut.
suggested_refs: The National Geographic Society's 1928 recognition of the ride

stops.name: Fifth Avenue, New York: the arrival
stops.date_confidence: attested to 20 September 1928. Total distance and stage count are contested: 21,500 km in 504 stages, or about 17,000 km in 494 stages, depending on the source. The widely reprinted interval of three years, four months and six days is an inherited arithmetic error; from 24 April 1925 the elapsed time is three years and 149 days
stops.campa: He rides Mancha up Fifth Avenue in gaucho dress with the Argentine colours in a rosette on his chest, and Mayor James J. Walker meets him with a gold medal and a ticker-tape parade. Three years and one hundred and forty-nine days out of Palermo. Gato is not there, and the animal that carried the last three thousand miles alone is a gelding of nineteen who was bred on frozen grass in Patagonia by people the Argentine army had spent a generation displacing. The newspaper at home says he arrives carrying the dust of twenty nations.
stops.quote: el polvo de veinte naciones... y sobre su pecho, en moño blanco y celeste... los colores argentinos
stops.quote_source: Mónica Stork, 'La travesía de Gato y Mancha' (2011), quoting the La Nación editorial of 23 September 1928
suggested_refs: La Nación editorial of 23 September 1928 on the New York arrival

stops.name: Madison Square Garden, Eighth Avenue: the horses on show
stops.date_confidence: weakly attested and contested: Infobae reports an exhibition of several days at an equestrian exposition, the ten-day figure rests on that source alone, and the Long Riders' Guild describes the New York honours without mentioning a Garden showing. Coordinates are those of the third Madison Square Garden on Eighth Avenue between 49th and 50th Streets, the building standing in 1928
stops.campa: The two horses, reunited, are put on show in New York before the voyage home. The building is the third Madison Square Garden, on Eighth Avenue, and it is not the one that stands under that name now. American crowds queue to look at two undersized geldings from Patagonia with roman noses and thick necks. In 1925 Argentine breeders were losing to imported blood and the criollo was being bred out. In 1928 New Yorkers pay at a turnstile to look at two of them.
suggested_refs: The third Madison Square Garden, Eighth Avenue between 49th and 50th Streets, 1925-1968
sources: Infobae, 'La osada travesía de Gato y Mancha'

stops.name: Dársena Norte, Buenos Aires: the horses come home by sea
stops.date_confidence: attested to 20 December 1928 by Infobae (2022 and 2023) and La Nación (2025), aboard the steamer Pan America. A reported 1 December departure from New York is not corroborated in the consulted sources
stops.campa: Mancha and Gato land at Dársena Norte to crowds on the quay, having come back the way the road would not let them go, by ship. They went north for three years on their own hooves and come south in a ship's hold in a few weeks. The city that called the plan lunacy three and a half years ago turns out in numbers to meet two horses. Tschiffely, who left as a temporary headmaster with holiday maps, comes back as the most famous foreigner in Argentina and has no job to go to.
suggested_refs: The steamer Pan America and the Dársena Norte arrival of 20 December 1928
sources: Infobae, 'La osada travesía de Gato y Mancha'

stops.name: Estancia El Cardal, the horses retired
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1929; no month or day is given in any consulted source
stops.campa: Mancha and Gato go back to Solanet's land near Ayacucho and are turned out for good, in the care of Juan Dindart. They are never worked again and never separated. Solanet's daughter Emma, born in 1934, grows up on this estancia and rides Mancha at a walk as a small girl. The horse under her is the one that crossed the Andes above five thousand metres and the Peruvian sand at fifty-two degrees, nine years before she was born. Tschiffely goes to London to write the thing down.
suggested_refs: Estancia El Cardal and Juan Dindart, keeper of the two horses

stops.name: London, the book and the marriage
stops.date_confidence: the book is attested to 1933 without a month; the marriage to Violet Marquesita is attested to December 1933, and the place is presumed London rather than documented
stops.campa: Tschiffely's Ride: Ten Thousand Miles in the Saddle from Southern Cross to Pole Star is published in London and sells enormously, and is translated into German, French, Finnish and Polish. He wrote it himself, in English, his third language. In December he marries the radio performer Violet Marquesita. The following year he publishes The Tale of Two Horses, told from the animals' point of view; some accounts date it 1935 and call it A Tale of Two Horses, and both are wrong. He settles in London as a full-time writer.
suggested_refs: Tschiffely's Ride (1933) and The Tale of Two Horses (1934), with the Long Riders' Guild reissues
sources: The Long Riders' Guild author page

stops.name: Estancia El Cardal, the reunion
stops.date_confidence: attested to the 1937 South American journey, written up in This Way Southward; the book is dated 1940 by one source and 1945 by another, and no month is given for the reunion
stops.campa: He comes back to South America to drive the length of the continent to Tierra del Fuego, and on the way he stops at El Cardal. The two horses are in a field and do not react to a stranger walking toward them. Then he calls their names. Nine years after New York, both heads come up and both animals come over, and one of them lifts a foreleg at the snap of a finger, a trick learned somewhere on a road between Bolivia and Texas that nobody has asked for since.
stops.quote: They made no response, but when I shouted their names, both at once looked up and came towards me.
stops.quote_source: A.F. Tschiffely, This Way Southward, quoted in Horse Canada, 'Tschiffely and the 10,000-Mile, Three-Year Ride: Part II'
suggested_refs: This Way Southward, Norton & Co., New York: the reunion chapter

stops.name: Estancia El Cardal, the two deaths
stops.date_confidence: attested: Gato dies 17 February 1944 aged 36 and Mancha dies 24 December 1947 aged 40 (Stork 2011, Infobae, Spanish Wikipedia, Camino Pampa). A '32 and 37' variant circulates in summary form and is attested nowhere in the consulted sources
stops.campa: Gato dies on the seventeenth of February 1944 at thirty-six. Mancha outlives him by nearly four years and dies on Christmas Eve 1947 at forty, an age at which most horses have been dead for two decades. They are buried in the park of the estancia. Solanet, who bought their grandparents from a Tehuelche cacique in 1911 and gave them away in 1925 to prove a point about a breed, has them both in his ground. Thirty-three years separate the purchase on the Chubut steppe from the first of the two graves at Ayacucho.
suggested_refs: The horses' graves in the park at Estancia El Cardal

stops.name: Museo del Transporte, Luján: the hides mounted
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the taxidermy is attested, the date is not given in any consulted source. The pin is the Complejo Museográfico Enrique Udaondo beside the Basilica of Luján
stops.campa: On Solanet's instruction the hides are preserved and mounted rather than going into the ground with the rest, and the two horses stand today in the Museo del Transporte at Luján, beside Tschiffely's memorabilia and a century of carriages. It is often said the horses lie at Recoleta; they do not, and never did. Their bones are at Ayacucho and their skins are at Luján. The Recoleta association belongs to the man, and it will only last forty-four years.
suggested_refs: Museo del Transporte, Complejo Museográfico Provincial Enrique Udaondo, Lezica y Torrezuri 917, Luján

stops.name: Chelsea, London: Emma Solanet finds him
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1953; no month or day is given, and the Chelsea coordinates are for the district, not a documented address
stops.campa: Emma Solanet, who rode Mancha as a child in the paddock at El Cardal, calls on the aging Tschiffely at Chelsea. She is nineteen. He is fifty-eight and has spent twenty years living off a book about her father's horses, in a city four continents away from the field where she first sat on one. It is the last documented meeting between the two families. Within a year he will be in a hospital in the East End for a routine operation, and the ashes will be going the other way down the Atlantic.
suggested_refs: Emma Solanet's 1953 visit, recounted in La Nación (2025)
sources: La Nación, 'La épica de Mancha y Gato...' (2025)

stops.name: Mile End Hospital, London: the death
stops.date_confidence: attested to 5 January 1954. Age at death is 58, not the 60 given in some summaries: born 7 May 1895
stops.campa: He enters Mile End Hospital shortly before Christmas 1953 for a very minor and routine operation and dies there on the fifth of January, aged fifty-eight. The man who crossed the altiplano at five thousand nine hundred metres, the Peruvian sand at fifty-two degrees, and the Cerro de la Muerte in cloud, dies in an East London ward after surgery nobody thought worth reporting. His widow Violeta will take charge of his papers and those of his friend Robert Bontine Cunninghame Graham.
suggested_refs: Mile End Hospital, London: admission and death records of December 1953 to January 1954

stops.name: Cementerio de la Recoleta, the gaucho funeral
stops.date_confidence: attested to 13 November 1954. Whether the urn stayed in one place at Recoleta for the whole forty-four years, or was moved within the cemetery first, is not settled by any consulted source
stops.campa: His remains are flown to Argentina and arrive on the thirteenth of November, and Buenos Aires buries the Swiss schoolmaster in Recoleta with a gaucho tribute. He lies in the necropolis of the Argentine state, among presidents and generals and, twenty-two years later, Eva Perón. He is a foreigner who taught English composition in Quilmes, and the republic has put him in its most exclusive ground for the crime of riding two of its horses to New York. He will not be left there.
suggested_refs: The November 1954 gaucho funeral tribute at Recoleta
sources: El Día, 'La increíble epopeya del jinete Tschiffely y de Mancha y Gato' (2025)

stops.name: Estancia El Cardal, Ayacucho: the ashes come back to the horses
stops.date_confidence: attested to 22 February 1998. The estancia's exact pin is not publicly documented; the coordinates are those used for Ayacucho throughout this journey
stops.campa: Forty-four years after his death, in accordance with his last wishes, the ashes leave Recoleta and are buried at El Cardal in a small templete facing the graves of Mancha and Gato. This is not where the ride began; the ride began at the Sociedad Rural in Palermo, three hundred kilometres north. This is where the horses came to him. A monument to the three of them stands in Plaza Colón in the town of Ayacucho, and since 1999 Argentina has kept the twentieth of September, the day Mancha reached Fifth Avenue, as the Día del Caballo.
suggested_refs: The templete at Estancia El Cardal and the monument in Plaza Colón, Ayacucho
sources: La Verdad de Ayacucho, 'El Cardal: obsequio a la vista y tributo a la historia'
